docs.title: SafeRS Native Public API
docs.text:
This site documents the public scripting / plugin API, exposed in two mirror forms:

  • C++ — srs::api::*, for plugins compiled against OSRSClient.lib. Headers live in OSRSClient/PluginAPI/API/. Plugins implement IScript (OSRSClient/PluginAPI/IScript.h) and call API methods, passing the ScriptContext& they receive in onLoad / pulse / onTick / onDraw.
  • Lua — srs.*, for .lua scripts loaded by the in-process Lua VM. Bindings live in OSRSClient/ScriptEngine/ScriptAPI.cpp. The host builds the ScriptContext internally; scripts just call srs.<module>.<method>(args).

The two forms are at feature parity — every method documented here is callable from both C++ and Lua. Differences in shape (where unavoidable, e.g. Lua lacks pointer semantics) are called out per-method.

Threading and spoofing contract

All action-firing methods (interact, attack, click, cast, …) route through Interact on the engine main thread with always-on input spoofing. There is no escape hatch — calling DoAction from the render thread crashes, and the spoofer is fail-closed (if it can't inject, the action drops).

docs.title: C++ — IScript
docs.text:
class IScript {
public:
    virtual const char* name() const = 0;
    virtual bool onLoad(const ScriptContext& ctx) = 0;
    virtual void onUnload() = 0;

    virtual void pulse  (const ScriptContext& ctx) {}  // per frame (~60Hz)
    virtual void onTick (const ScriptContext& ctx) {}  // per game tick (~600ms)
    virtual void onDraw (const ScriptContext& ctx) {}  // per frame, inside ImGui frame

    virtual void onSettingsChanged(const nlohmann::json& settings) {}
    virtual nlohmann::json schema() const { return {}; }
};

Plugins export CreateScript / DestroyScript functions and ship as DLLs in the plugins/ directory.

To defer a one-shot to the next game tick from inside pulse, call ctx.tickScheduler->onNext(fn) — see nextTick / onNext below.

docs.title: Lua — callback registration
docs.text:
script.pulse(function() ... end)     -- per frame
script.onTick(function() ... end)    -- per game tick
script.nextTick(function() ... end)  -- one-shot, fires on the next tick only
script.draw(function() ... end)      -- per frame, inside ImGui frame

script.draw is the only callback where srs.draw.* calls are valid — the host guarantees a live ImGui frame for it. pulse, onTick, and nextTick do not.

docs.title: Metadata and settings
docs.text: The launcher's sidebar treats C++ plugins and Lua scripts uniformly — both can declare display metadata (name, author, version, description) and a settings schema that the launcher renders as an editable form.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Without a metadata declaration, a Lua script shows up in the sidebar under its filename stem with v * * "lua" and empty version / size. To override, call script.declareInfo once at the top level:

script.declareInfo {
    name        = "Power Miner",        -- overrides filename stem
    author      = "you",
    version     = "1.0.0",
    description = "Mines essence at Power-mine, drops at threshold.",
}

All fields are optional. C++ plugins set the equivalent fields via REGISTER_CORE_PLUGIN(...) (or external-plugin metadata) and the IScript::name() virtual.

docs.title: Settings schema
docs.text:
Both IScript::schema() and script.declareSettings accept the same shape — a list of groups, each with a list of rows. The launcher renders each row as a typed input (check, select, number, slider) and ships the user's edits back to the plugin / script.

script.declareSettings {
    groups = {
        { id = "general", title = "general", open = true, rows = {
            { id = "mode",      label = "Protect mode",   kind = "select",
              value = "Auto", options = { "Auto", "Magic", "Range", "Melee" } },
            { id = "lookahead", label = "Tick lookahead", kind = "number",
              value = 1, min = 0, max = 3 },
            { id = "smite",     label = "Use Smite",      kind = "check",
              value = false },
        }},
        { id = "display", title = "display", open = true, rows = {
            { id = "opacity",   label = "Overlay opacity", kind = "slider",
              value = 80, min = 0, max = 100 },
        }},
    },
}

The C++ equivalent returns the same JSON shape from IScript::schema():

nlohmann::json schema() const override {
    return nlohmann::json::parse(R"json({
        "groups": [
            { "id": "general", "title": "general", "open": true, "rows": [
                { "id": "mode", "label": "Protect mode", "kind": "select",
                  "value": "Auto",
                  "options": ["Auto", "Magic", "Range", "Melee"] }
            ]}
        ]
    })json");
}
kind Renders as Extra fields check checkbox value: bool select dropdown value, options: [...] number numeric input value, min, max slider slider value, min, max

Without a declareSettings / schema() call, the sidebar shows just the master enable toggle and no rows.

docs.title: Reading values
docs.text:
User edits are flattened by the launcher to "<groupId>.<rowId>" keys before crossing the IPC boundary, so a script reads its own setting under that combined key:

script.onSettingsChanged(function(s)
    print("protect mode:", s["general.mode"])
    print("smite on:",     s["general.smite"])
end)

-- Snapshot read at call time:
local s = script.settings()
if s["general.smite"] then ... end

The C++ onSettingsChanged(const nlohmann::json&) receives the same flat-keyed object. The launcher pushes the current values to the plugin / script on enable, on every edit, and after a hot reload — handlers should be idempotent.

Identity

A script's settings are persisted by the launcher under the script's id, derived from the filename stem. Renaming the .lua file orphans its saved values. Pick a name you're willing to keep, and avoid renaming group / row ids in the schema between releases for the same reason.

docs.title: pulse vs onTick
docs.text:
Callback Cadence Use for pulse every rendered frame (~60 Hz) cheap state checks, per-frame visual work onTick every game tick (~600 ms) action firing, state-machine transitions

Move action logic to onTick and use pulse only for checks.

docs.title: nextTick / onNext
docs.text:
nextTick (Lua) / tickScheduler->onNext (C++) bridge fast pulse detection to server-aligned firing: evaluate a condition inside pulse (~60Hz so you don't miss a short-lived window), and when it fires, queue a closure to run on the very next game tick, then drop it.

Each call queues exactly one callback. The host drains the queue once per tick after the regular onTick fan, so steady-state tick handlers always run first. A re-queue from inside a deferred callback lands on the next tick, not this one.

Property Behavior Cadence one-shot — fires on the next tick rollover, then dropped Order after onTick, before the BreakManager scheduler Pause / disable owning plugin/script disabled or paused before drain → callback is silently dropped (same gating as pulse / onTick) Re-entrancy onNext called from inside a deferred fn schedules for the NEXT tick ImGui frame not guaranteed — call srs.draw.* only from script.draw / onDraw

When to use each:

  • Always firing every tick? Use onTick.
  • Need fast detection (a projectile, a hitsplat, a tick-aligned animation start) but the action itself must land aligned to the server? Detect in pulse, defer with nextTick / onNext.
  • Per-frame visual work? Use pulse (state) + draw / onDraw (paint).

docs.title: Lua example
docs.text:
-- Detect the "tick-eat" window in pulse (need ≥60Hz to catch it),
-- then fire the eat exactly once on the next tick.
local pending = false
script.pulse(function()
    if not pending and srs.player.hpPercent() < 35 then
        pending = true
        script.nextTick(function()
            srs.inventory.interact("Shark", "Eat")
            pending = false
        end)
    end
end)

docs.title: C++ example
docs.text:
void pulse(const ScriptContext& ctx) override {
    using namespace srs::api;
    if (!m_pending && Player::hpPercent(ctx) < 35) {
        m_pending = true;
        ctx.tickScheduler->onNext([this, &ctx]{
            Inventory::interact(ctx, "Shark", "Eat");
            m_pending = false;
        });
    }
}

The m_pending flag prevents queueing the same action 36× across the ~600 ms tick window before nextTick actually fires. Without it, every pulse between detection and the next tick would push another copy of the closure onto the queue.

Lifetime of captured pointers

ScriptContext references stay valid for the lifetime of the enabled plugin/script. Capturing ctx by reference in a closure is safe because the deferred callback is dropped if the owning plugin/script is disabled before the drain runs. Do not capture raw pointers into game-state nodes that may rotate between ticks (e.g. an NpcInstance* from EntityQuery) — re-resolve from ctx inside the closure body.

docs.title: Example — minimal Lua script
docs.text:
-- Drop every shrimp the moment it lands in the backpack.
script.onTick(function()
    if srs.inventory.contains("Shrimps") then
        srs.inventory.dropAll("Shrimps")
    end
end)

script.draw(function()
    if srs.draw.beginAnchoredOverlay(
            "##fish-hud", 162, 32,
            srs.Corner.TopRight, -4, 4) then
        srs.draw.text("Caught: " .. srs.inventory.count("Shrimps"))
        srs.draw.endOverlay()
    end
end)

docs.title: Example — minimal C++ plugin
docs.text:
class FishingPlugin : public IScript {
public:
    const char* name() const override { return "Fishing"; }
    bool onLoad(const ScriptContext&) override { return true; }
    void onUnload() override {}

    void onTick(const ScriptContext& ctx) override {
        using namespace srs::api;
        if (Inventory::contains(ctx, "Shrimps")) {
            Inventory::dropAll(ctx, "Shrimps");
        }
    }

    void onDraw(const ScriptContext& ctx) override {
        using namespace srs::api;
        if (Drawing::beginAnchoredOverlay(ctx, "##fish-hud",
                                          162, 32,
                                          Drawing::Corner::TopRight,
                                          -4, 4)) {
            Drawing::text("Caught: " + std::to_string(
                Inventory::count(ctx, std::string("Shrimps"))));
            Drawing::endOverlay();
        }
    }
};

extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) IScript* CreateScript()  { return new FishingPlugin(); }
extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) void DestroyScript(IScript* s) { delete s; }

docs.title: Antiban
docs.text:
srs::api::Antiban / srs.antiban

Human-like timing + idle behavior. Designed for onTick:

C++Lua 
void onTick(const ScriptContext& ctx) override {
    using namespace srs::api;
    if (Antiban::shouldDelay(ctx))      return;
    if (Antiban::shouldMicroBreak())    return;
    if (workIsDone()) {
        Antiban::moveMouseRandomly(ctx);
        return;
    }
    performAction(ctx);
    Antiban::recordAction();
}

script.onTick(function()
    if srs.antiban.shouldDelay()      then return end
    if srs.antiban.shouldMicroBreak() then return end
    if workIsDone() then
        srs.antiban.moveMouseRandomly()
        return
    end
    performAction()
    srs.antiban.recordAction()
end)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• shouldDelay's fatigue argument is the per-call skip probability (0..1). Default 5%; pass higher values during long sessions to slow the script down.
  • shouldMicroBreak's default of 0.1 % at 60 Hz works out to roughly one break per ~16 seconds of polling.
  • moveMouseRandomly reads the live viewport size from Camera::state(); falls back to (1024, 768) if the camera hasn't initialized.
  • The three total* counters are diagnostic — they feed the debug panel readout and are handy for script HUDs / logging.

srs::api::Area / srs.area

Player-position area-containment checks. 2D only — plane is ignored. Add a plane-aware overload when an actual use case appears.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Form C++ Lua Inside inclusive rect Area::isWithin(ctx, x1, y1, x2, y2) → bool srs.area.isWithin(x1, y1, x2, y2) → bool Within Chebyshev radius Area::isWithin(ctx, cx, cy, tilesAway) → bool srs.area.isWithin(cx, cy, tilesAway) → bool In an instance Area::isInInstance(ctx) → bool srs.area.isInInstance() → bool
  • Rect form — (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) are opposing corners. Either pair works (upper-left + lower-right, upper-right + lower-left, etc.) — internally min/max-ed against each axis.
  • Radius form — tilesAway is inclusive (player on the boundary counts as inside). tilesAway = 0 means "exactly on the tile".

Lua dispatches by arity: 4 args = rect, 3 args = radius.

isInInstance returns true when the current scene is a real instance (a private boss arena, raid, minigame lobby, …), read from the engine's in-instance flag; false when that flag can't be resolved. Pairs with srs.player.templatePosition() for instance-aware coordinate handling.

docs.title: Bank PIN
docs.text:
Auto-enter the bound account's 4-digit PIN on the keypad. The PIN itself is stored in the launcher's per-account encrypted record (DPAPI, user-scope) and never crosses the script API boundary — handleBankPin takes no PIN argument and hasBoundBankPin only exposes a boolean. The DLL leases the PIN through osrs::breakmgr::CredentialStore::leaseBankPin(), dispatches four CC_OP (slot 57) clicks on the keypad widgets in group 213, and zeros the buffer before returning.

Method C++ Lua Auto-enter the PIN Bank::handleBankPin(ctx) → bool srs.bank.handleBankPin() → bool Has a PIN been bound Bank::hasBoundBankPin() → bool srs.bank.hasBoundBankPin() → bool

Per-call flow (one keypad click per pulse — tick-driven):

  1. Bail with true (no-op success) if the PIN widget isn't open.
  2. Bail with false if no account is bound, the account has no PIN, or the keypad's digit labels haven't been populated yet (the engine's CS2 script that writes them runs on the next engine tick after the keypad opens — see "Why tick-driven" below).
  3. Read widget (213, 10) to determine which digit position the keypad is currently asking for (FIRST / SECOND / THIRD / FOURTH). Bail with false if the text doesn't match yet (engine mid-update).
  4. Lease the PIN, look up the digit char for the current position, scan the keypad letter slots' dynamic children for one whose text matches.
  5. Prime the mouse-spoof ring + write the LL-hook AFK timestamps, then synthesize a WM_MOUSEMOVE / WM_LBUTTONDOWN / WM_LBUTTONUP sequence on the game window via the engine's own WndProc. The engine's input pipeline emits the natural MOUSE_MOVE_1/2 + CLICK_1/2 + CC_OP packet on its next tick.
  6. Drop the lease (destructor zeros the PIN bytes).

Why tick-driven: when the script itself opened the bank, the queued DoAction for the banker click and the CS2 script that writes the keypad's digit labels both run on the engine main thread — which is the same thread the script's pulse callback runs on. Blocking inside handleBankPin (via sleep_for) starves the engine of the very frames it needs to populate those labels, so the wait would time out even though the keypad is visible. Each call now returns in <1 ms with no blocking; the script re-polls every tick until the widget closes.

Why WndProc synth instead of the packet path: real-player keypad clicks route through the dyn child's wrapper pointer (verified via live packet capture 2026-05-23), but Interact::resolveWidget(group, child) returns the static parent's wrapper. The packet path produced silently-dropped packets. Letting the engine's own input pipeline turn a WndProc click into the wire packet bypasses that mismatch and matches real-player wire bytes — same mechanism Tab::switchTo and Interact::walkToMinimapPoint use.

Return values:

  • true — PIN widget isn't open (no-op) or a click was dispatched this tick.
  • false — no account bound, account has no PIN, keypad labels aren't populated yet, instruction text doesn't match a known phrase, the digit widget can't be found in group 213, or the WndProc hook isn't installed yet.

Calling pattern — call every pulse while the PIN widget is open:

script.pulse(function()
  if srs.bank.isPinOpen() then
    if not srs.bank.hasBoundBankPin() then
      log.info("Bind an account with a PIN via the launcher Accounts panel")
      return
    end
    srs.bank.handleBankPin()
  end
end)

To set a PIN for an account, open the launcher's Accounts modal, enter a 4-digit PIN in the "Bank PIN" field, and save. The PIN is encrypted alongside the password and only the bound game tab can read it back (DPAPI user-scope + per-binary entropy salt).

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
The bank has 10 tabs: 0 = "All Items" (∞ icon), 1..9 = user-configurable. Current tab lives in varbit BANK_CURRENTTAB (4150). Most scrolling / per-item flows operate on the All Items view — Bank::scrollToSlot auto-switches to it if you're on another tab.

Method C++ Lua Current tab Bank::currentTab(ctx) → int (0..9) srs.bank.currentTab() → int Open a specific tab Bank::openTab(ctx, idx) → bool srs.bank.openTab(idx) → bool Open All Items (∞) Bank::openMainTab(ctx) → bool srs.bank.openMainTab() → bool

Tab clicks route as CC_OP (slot 57) packets at widget (12, 10) with subSlot = 10 + tabIndex*4, identifier = 1, itemId = 0xFFFF — matches real-player wire bytes captured 2026-05-19.

docs.title: Container reads
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua All slots Bank::all(ctx) → vector<InventoryItem> srs.bank.all() → table Contains by id Bank::contains(ctx, id) → bool srs.bank.contains(id) → bool Contains by name Bank::contains(ctx, name) → bool srs.bank.contains(name) → bool Count by id Bank::count(ctx, id) → int32 srs.bank.count(id) → int Count by name Bank::count(ctx, name) → int32 srs.bank.count(name) → int

Name lookups match the item's in-game display name (case- and whitespace-insensitive substring). contains("prayer potion") matches all 4 dose variants because every dose string contains it.

Bank slot index

The slot field on items returned from Bank::all is the bank container index (0..hundreds), not a backpack 0..27 index. The container is laid out in tab order — slots [0..N1-1] for tab 1, then [N1..N1+N2-1] for tab 2, ..., then untabbed (tab 0) at the end. The "All Items" visual view renders untabbed FIRST with partial-row breaks between sections — scrollToSlot does the visual-row math for you.

docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Scroll a slot into view Bank::scrollToSlot(ctx, slotIndex) → bool srs.bank.scrollToSlot(slot) → bool Mouse-wheel notches Bank::scrollWheel(ctx, notches) → bool srs.bank.scrollWheel(n) → bool Raw widget scrollY read — srs.widget.scrollY(g, c) → int or nil Raw widget scrollY write — srs.widget.setScrollY(g, c, y) → bool

scrollToSlot is the high-level helper: it auto-switches to the All Items tab if needed, computes the visual row accounting for tab partial-row breaks, and fires Microbot's trio (setVarcInt(BANK_SCROLL, y) + runScript(UPDATE_SCROLLBAR, ...) + direct IfType+0x88 write). Returns true if the row is already in view (no-op).

scrollWheel synthesizes WM_MOUSEWHEEL events over the bank center — positive notches scroll DOWN, negative UP. Blocks ~16 ms per notch.

docs.text:
All variants route a CC_OP (slot 57) packet at widget (12, 12) — Bankmain.ITEMS — with subSlot = bank slot index, itemId from the container at that slot, and the menu identifier per quantity. The caller picks the item by id or by name (case-insensitive partial match).

docs.title: Per-item deposit
docs.text:
The deposit-side inventory inside the bank window is widget (15, 3) (Bankside.ITEMS). Clicks route as CC_OP (slot 57) at that widget with subSlot = backpack slot (0..27), itemId from the backpack cache, and Deposit-All identifier 2 (the deposit-side op ordering differs from the withdraw side — see Bank.cpp fireDepositSlotClick).

depositAllExcept fires Deposit-All on the FIRST non-kept inventory slot per call and returns false; the script polls each tick until only kept items remain, at which point it returns true.

Unverified: the bank's deposit ops may follow the quantity preset. The deposit box's item ops turned out to be positional — op 1 is whichever quantity the preset selects, so its Deposit-All constant only held on the preset it was captured under (see DepositBox, fixed there). The bank's identifier 2 was confirmed live but we don't know on which preset. If the same model applies, 2 stays Deposit-All for every preset except ALL, where depositAllExcept would deposit one item per click. Until that's measured, treat a bank quantity preset of All as untested — the header comment on fireDepositSlotClick in Bank.cpp lists the experiment that settles it.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
srs::api::Breaks / srs.breaks

Script/plugin-facing surface for the BreakManager — schedule, observe, and react to break cycles (work → request → logout → idle → login → recover).

Credentials are sandboxed

Scripts can not see or set credentials — those are owned by SafeRSClient's AccountStore and the DLL-internal CredentialStore. Scripts can only observe state, request/skip breaks, and subscribe to phase events.

Auto-pause / resume

The Scheduler pauses scripts during a break; their pulse / onTick callbacks just stop firing. Scripts don't need to call setPaused on themselves.

docs.text:

Skip the next scheduled break (one-shot) Breaks::skipNextBreak() srs.breaks.skipNextBreak() Recover from a failed login cycle Breaks::resetFromFailed() srs.breaks.resetFromFailed() Hop to a world after each relogin (0 / -1 = off) Breaks::setHopWorld(world) srs.breaks.setHopWorld(world) Provide the relogin hop world via callback Breaks::setHopWorldProvider(fn) —

setHopWorld / setHopWorldProvider make the BreakManager hop to a different world when it logs back in after a break. The provider form takes a callback returning the target world each relogin (return <= 0 to skip) and supersedes the fixed setHopWorld; a 0 / negative value disables hopping. setHopWorldProvider is C++-facade only.

docs.title: Break handshake
docs.text:
For scripts that need to reach a safe state (banked, out of combat, etc.) before they get paused:

  1. Call declareBreakAware() once (from onTick / onLoad / pulse) to register as a script the Scheduler will wait on.
  2. Check isBreakRequested() each tick during normal work.
  3. Once safe, call signalReady() — idempotent, fine every tick.
Method C++ Lua Has a break been requested? Breaks::isBreakRequested() → bool srs.breaks.isBreakRequested() → bool Opt this script into the wait set Breaks::declareBreakAware() srs.breaks.declareBreakAware() Mark this script ready for break Breaks::signalReady() srs.breaks.signalReady()

Caller attribution + no grace timeout

Handshake calls must be made from inside an onTick / pulse / onDraw callback — the Scheduler reads the currently-firing script index for attribution. Calls from outside any callback (e.g. top-level chunk during loadFile) won't attribute correctly and are silently dropped.

There is no grace timeout: a script that opts in but never signals will block every future break. Don't declareBreakAware unless you intend to signal.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
Timing-only (no credential fields).

Method C++ Lua Read Breaks::profile() → Profile srs.breaks.getProfile() → table Write (declarative — omitted keys reset to defaults) Breaks::setProfile(Profile) srs.breaks.setProfile(table)

setProfile is declarative

setProfile does not merge into the current profile: any key you omit from the table resets to its default (the column below), not to its previously-set value. A script calling srs.breaks.setProfile({workMinutesMin = 40}) silently resets everything else — including logoutDuringBreak — back to defaults. To tweak one field, read getProfile(), mutate the returned table, and pass the whole table back:

local p = srs.breaks.getProfile()
p.workMinutesMin = 40
srs.breaks.setProfile(p)

Camera
docs.text:
srs::api::Camera / srs.camera

DreamBot-style camera facade: read pitch / yaw / zoom and rotate or zoom the view. rotateTo* snaps instantly via a direct memory write to the engine's target angles, keyboardRotateTo* drives human-looking arrow-key holds, and setZoom converges by injecting WM_MOUSEWHEEL events.

Plugin facade vs. GameSDK Camera

This is the plugin-API facade for camera control. Internal engine access via OSRSClient/GameSDK/Camera.h (low-level state) is not part of the public API — use srs::api::Camera from plugins and scripts.

docs.title: Rotation modes
docs.text:
Three "modes" are exposed via three method families:

Family Mechanism Notes rotateTo* Direct write to engine TargetPitch / TargetYaw Instant, no smoothing. Cheap and reliable. Default. keyboardRotateTo* Arrow-key holds through InputManager Slower, human-looking. For antiban scenarios. mouseRotateTo* DreamBot uses scroll-wheel here OSRS scroll is bound to zoom, not yaw, so this falls back to the direct memory path on this client. Kept for source compatibility with ported scripts.

Hold duration on keyboardRotateTo* is proportional to angle delta; capped at ~2.5 s per call so a runaway rotation doesn't lock the keyboard for the script.

docs.text:

How zoom works

OSRS has no user-zoom integer — camera distance derives from pitch + viewport. getZoom returns a value normalized to DreamBot's [330, 3000] range, and setZoom reaches a target by injecting WM_MOUSEWHEEL events (see Zoom below). Convergence is best-effort: setZoom returns false if it can't settle within tolerance.

docs.title: Rotation (default — memory write)
docs.text:
All rotateTo* calls clamp pitch to [128, 383] and mask yaw with & 0x7FF before writing. Return true on a successful write, false if the camera state isn't resolved or the write faults.

Method C++ Lua Both axes Camera::rotateTo(ctx, yaw, pitch) → bool srs.camera.rotateTo(yaw, pitch) → bool Yaw only Camera::rotateToYaw(ctx, yaw) → bool srs.camera.rotateToYaw(yaw) → bool Pitch only Camera::rotateToPitch(ctx, pitch) → bool srs.camera.rotateToPitch(pitch) → bool Face a tile Camera::rotateToTile(ctx, tile) → bool srs.camera.rotateToTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Face an entity Camera::rotateToEntity(ctx, target) → bool srs.camera.rotateToEntity(target) → bool

Interrupt-condition overloads (C++): rotateToTile and rotateToEntity accept a Predicate interrupt polled between micro-steps. Return true from it to abort early.

Lua (x, y[, plane]) overloads

Every tile-taking camera function accepts raw coordinates in Lua — rotateToTile(tile), rotateToTile(x, y), or rotateToTile(x, y, plane) — and the same applies to mouseRotateToTile, keyboardRotateToTile, getYawForTile, getPitchForTile, and rotateToTileEvent. This matters because WorldTile has no Lua constructor: a script that didn't get a tile from an API like srs.player.position() must use the coordinate form.

docs.title: Ensure visible
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Ensure a tile is on-screen Camera::ensureVisible(ctx, tile) → bool srs.camera.ensureVisible(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Ensure an entity is on-screen Camera::ensureVisible(ctx, target) → bool srs.camera.ensureVisible(target) → bool

Opt-in helper to call before a canvas click: a no-op returning true when the target already projects to visible pixels, otherwise it rotates via rotateToTile / rotateToEntity. Returns false only when camera state can't be read or the rotation faults. A true does not guarantee same-frame projection — the engine renders one frame after the angle write, so the pixel lands on-screen next frame.

The Lua binding follows the same overload family as rotateToTile: ensureVisible(tile), ensureVisible(target), ensureVisible(x, y) (plane 0), or ensureVisible(x, y, plane).

docs.title: Example
Chat
docs.text:
srs::api::Chat / srs.chat

Read the game chatbox as an event stream. Every line the engine adds funnels through one native choke point, so a single subscription observes them all: server game / system messages (the minigame and boss status lines), public player chat, private messages, clan / friends-chat, broadcasts, and the friend login/out notifier. This is the native equivalent of RuneLite's ChatMessage event. There is no polling reader — chat is delivered only as events.

System vs. player messages

sender is empty for server/system (game) messages and non-empty for player chat. That is the robust way to tell a minigame/boss status line from someone actually talking — prefer it over matching on type, since server game messages are server-driven and don't carry one fixed type value.

Callback thread differs by language

The C++ callback runs on the game thread, synchronously inside the engine — keep it cheap and thread-safe. The Lua callback is delivered on the script thread (queued by the hook, drained once per frame), so it is safe to call the rest of the srs.* API from it. Per-script pause applies to the Lua path.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Subscribe to chat lines Chat::onMessage(cb) → uint64 srs.chat.onMessage(fn) → token Unsubscribe Chat::offMessage(token) srs.chat.offMessage(token) → bool

onMessage fires for every line, not just messages aimed at you — filter in your handler. Returns a token (0 in C++ if the hook isn't installed); pass it to offMessage to stop listening.

C++: process-wide, takes no ScriptContext. The callback (ChatMessageCallback = std::function<void(const ChatMessageEvent&)>) runs on the game thread.

Lua: fn receives a table {type, sender, message, channel, wallClock}.

Unsubscribing

srs.chat.offMessage(token) removes the callback registered under that token. It is safe to call from inside the callback itself. Returns false for an unknown or already-removed token. A full script reload clears all subscriptions automatically, so a register-once-at-load callback needs no explicit cleanup.

docs.title: Chat types
docs.text:
srs.chat.type.* — engine chat-type ints (RuneLite ChatMessageType values) to compare against event.type. GAMEMESSAGE and PUBLIC are verified live; the rest are from the reverse-engineering pass. Server / system messages do not use a single value — level-ups and examines arrive as GAMEMESSAGE (0), while filterable "spam" like eating or skilling comes through as 105, and broadcasts use others still. So the robust "is this a system line?" test is an empty sender (player chat always has a sender), not a type match. Log event.type to discover others on your build.

Constant Value Meaning GAMEMESSAGE 0 Server / system message — level-ups, examine (verified) PUBLIC 2 Local player public chat (verified) PRIVATE_IN 3 Private message received LOGIN_LOGOUT 5 "X has logged in/out." (friend notifier) MOD_PRIVATE 6 Private message from a Jagex mod PRIVATE_OUT 7 Private message you sent FRIENDS_CHAT 9 Friends-chat channel message CLAN_CHAT 41 Clan chat (unverified on this build) CLAN_GUEST_CHAT 42 Guest clan chat (unverified on this build) CONSOLE 99 In-game console / client widget log

Deposit-box variant of bank operations. Reads the player's inventory (container 93) directly — there's no separate "deposit-box container". Group 192 (BankDepositbox) hosts the buttons and the deposit-side item grid (child 24).

Same pattern as Bank: open (via the scene loc), close, bulk- deposit buttons, per-item depositAllExcept, and the quantity preset.

Verified from a live DoAction capture (build 239): slot=57 X=11 Y=12582913 "Close", i.e. (192, 1) subSlot 11 — the same shape as the bank's own close. Returns false if the box isn't open or the button isn't rendered this frame.

docs.title: Per-item deposit
docs.text:
The deposit-side inventory is widget (192, 24) — the box renders the player's backpack in its own grid (not the sidebar). These are UI/CS2 widget actions, so they dispatch as engine invokes (DoAction), not wire packets: a CC_OP (slot 57) at that widget with subSlot = backpack slot (0..27), itemId from the backpack cache, and op index 1 (spawnIdx).

Method C++ Lua Deposit all except (by id) DepositBox::depositAllExcept(ctx, vector<int32_t>) → bool srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({ids...}) → bool Deposit all except (by name) DepositBox::depositAllExcept(ctx, vector<string>) → bool srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({"names"...}) → bool

depositAllExcept fires one deposit click on the FIRST non-kept inventory slot per call and returns false; the script polls each tick until only kept items remain, at which point it returns true.

docs.title: The item ops are positional
docs.text:
The box's item ops are positional: op index 1 is whichever quantity the quantity preset currently selects — not literally Deposit-All — and the action string passed along with the click is cosmetic, since only the index dispatches. A click labelled "Deposit-All" therefore deposits a single item while the preset says 1, which is what the box opens on.

depositAllExcept handles this for you: before its first deposit click it reads the preset and, if it isn't ALL, clicks the All button and returns false. The next poll deposits normally — one extra tick per box visit, no blocking, and scripts never need to touch the preset themselves. A pack that is entirely kept items still returns true immediately without changing the preset.

If you fire the ops yourself rather than through depositAllExcept, select ALL first and check it landed with getQuantity — do not assume the identifiers from a capture taken on some other preset.

Keeping an in-inventory tool (e.g. a pickaxe) is the primary use case:

-- Bank ore at the deposit box while keeping the pickaxe in the pack.
if srs.depositbox.open() and srs.depositbox.isOpen() then
  if srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({ "Bronze pickaxe", "Gem bag" }) then
    srs.depositbox.close()
  end
end

docs.title: Quantity preset
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Set quantity DepositBox::setQuantity(ctx, q) → bool srs.depositbox.setQuantity(q) → bool Read quantity DepositBox::getQuantity(ctx) → optional<Quantity> srs.depositbox.getQuantity() → q \| nil

Quantity constants (DepositBox::Quantity / srs.depositbox.*): ONE, FIVE, TEN, X, ALL. Same set as Bank; the Shop Quantity enum differs — ONE / FIVE / TEN / FIFTY / X, no ALL — so don't reuse constants across the tables.

setQuantity clicks the matching 1/5/10/X/All button and needs the box open. getQuantity reads varbit DEPOSITBOX_MODE (4430) instead, so it works whether or not the box is open — the preset is sticky across visits. It returns nullopt / nil if the varbit can't be read. Use it rather than reading 4430 yourself: the raw values are not in button order (measured in-client 2026-07-14 — 1=0, 5=1, All=2, X=3, 10=4), so the mapping is not something to infer from the button layout.

-- The preset is sticky, so a script that fires the item ops directly
-- should confirm it rather than trust the box's default.
if srs.depositbox.getQuantity() ~= srs.depositbox.ALL then
  srs.depositbox.setQuantity(srs.depositbox.ALL)
  return  -- re-poll next tick; the click needs a tick to land
end

docs.title: Dialogue
docs.text:
srs::api::Dialogue / srs.dialogue

Detect and advance OSRS dialogue. Continue prompts use spacebar via KeyboardSpoofer (the engine's built-in keybind); option menus use number keys 1..9. Option 10+ requires a mouse click on the option row (not implemented here).

docs.title: ⚠️ A Messagebox is not a blocking gate
docs.text:
isOpen() does not mean "the game is waiting on you."

Widget group 229 (Messagebox) is an informational chatbox notice — e.g. "Your inventory is too full to hold any more pay-dirt." with a "Click here to continue" line. Unlike NPC chat it does not pause the game: your character keeps walking, mining and clicking while it's up, and almost any action (walking especially) clears it on its own.

So this idiom — which earlier versions of this page recommended — wedges your script forever the moment a Messagebox appears:

-- ❌ BROKEN: spins forever on a Messagebox.
if srs.dialogue.isOpen() then
    if srs.dialogue.hasContinue() then srs.dialogue.clickContinue() end
    return   -- nothing else ever runs
end

It fails silently and is nasty to diagnose: the state machine keeps reporting its intended state while the executor never runs, so every log line looks healthy. Gate blocking work on isOpen() and not isMessagebox() instead — see the example below.

hasContinue() is true for a Messagebox, and correctly so: 229 really does own a continue component (229.4 Messagebox.CONTINUE). It answers "does this dialogue have a continue arrow", not "is the game blocked". Use isMessagebox() to tell informational, ignore it from must advance.

docs.title: Widget groups
docs.text:
Groups (RuneLite gameval/InterfaceID.java), and which are advanceable with clickContinue:

Group Kind Blocks game? Advance with 229 Messagebox — plain text No — informational clickContinue (or just ignore it) 217 ChatRight — player dialogue (head on right) Yes clickContinue 231 ChatLeft — NPC dialogue (head on left) Yes clickContinue 60 ChatBoth — two-portrait Yes clickContinue 193 Objectbox — single-sprite Yes clickContinue (keystroke only) 11 ObjectboxDouble — two-sprite Yes clickContinue 219 Chatmenu — "Select an Option" menu Yes selectOption / selectOptionByText

Every group except 219 is a continue-style dialog, and hasContinue() is true for all of them. 219 is the only one that needs selectOption.

docs.title: Mechanism, and what clickContinue's return value means
docs.text:
clickContinue and selectOption post their keystroke through the engine's InputEventManager — the same keyPressed/keyChar/keyReleased trio the client's own window procedure posts for a real key press. They are fire-and-forget: they enqueue on the engine thread and return immediately.

true means "keystroke dispatched", not "dialogue advanced." Never treat the return value as confirmation. Poll isOpen() / hasContinue() on a later tick to see whether it landed, and give the dialogue a tick or two — a dialogue that is still up on the very next tick has not necessarily failed.

If a live test shows the keystroke doesn't take for some group, clickContinueByClick() does the same job with a real mouse click on the group's continue component. It blocks the calling script (mouse move + click drain), so keep clickContinue as the per-tick default and reach for the click only as a fallback.

docs.text:
Convenience names mirroring Microbot's Rs2Dialogue, available in both C++ and Lua — each is a thin wrapper:

Alias Same as isInDialogue() isOpen() hasSelectAnOption() hasOptions() continueSpace() clickContinue() clickOption(n) / clickOption(text) selectOption(n) / selectOptionByText(text)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Advance real dialogue, but never let an informational message stop the script working. The rule: only a non-Messagebox dialogue earns a return.

C++Lua 
using namespace srs::api;

// A Messagebox blocks nothing — nudge it and carry on working.
if (Dialogue::isMessagebox(ctx)) {
    Dialogue::clickContinue(ctx);
    // deliberately no return — walking clears it anyway
} else if (Dialogue::hasOptions(ctx)) {
    Dialogue::selectOptionByText(ctx, "Yes");
    return;                       // real dialogue: game is blocked
} else if (Dialogue::hasContinue(ctx)) {
    Dialogue::clickContinue(ctx);
    return;                       // real dialogue: game is blocked
}

-- A Messagebox blocks nothing — nudge it and carry on working.
if srs.dialogue.isMessagebox() then
    srs.dialogue.clickContinue()
    -- deliberately no return — walking clears it anyway
elseif srs.dialogue.hasOptions() then
    srs.dialogue.selectOptionByText("Yes")
    return                        -- real dialogue: game is blocked
elseif srs.dialogue.hasContinue() then
    srs.dialogue.clickContinue()
    return                        -- real dialogue: game is blocked
end

Because clickContinue reports dispatch rather than success, a script that must not stall on an unexpected dialogue should also cap how long it will keep trying — count consecutive ticks a dialogue has been open and fall through past a small budget, rather than returning forever.

docs.title: Example
Engine
docs.text:
srs::api::Engine / srs.engine

Engine-level introspection and low-level primitives. Two distinct surfaces live in the same Lua table:

  1. Action-cap introspection — observe the per-server-tick action counter that PacketSendHook maintains and GameData::onTick resets. Backs the official C++ API at srs::api::Engine.
  2. Diagnostic primitives — RuneLite-style client.* helpers (VarClient reads / writes, raw CS2 runScript, input-block toggle). Lua-only — no equivalent in srs::api::Engine because they're intended for one-shot RE / diagnostic probes, not production scripts.

Scripts MUST NOT block

pulse / onTick / draw handlers run on the engine main thread. To gate on action capacity, check canDispatchAction() and yield via script.nextTick(...) if it returns false — never spin-wait.

docs.title: Action-cap introspection
docs.text:
The OSRS server enforces a cap of 8 action-class packets per game cycle (vanilla). The DLL counts every action-class opcode that srs::engine::isAction() recognises — OpLoc*, OpNpc*, OpObj*, IfButton*, etc. — but not input-bundle traffic (mouse moves, clicks, key events, heartbeats). The actual gating happens automatically inside EngineDispatch::drainOnMainThread, so scripts can burst-fire actions (drop-all, mass-eat, gear-swap) without manually pacing.

These accessors exist purely for diagnostic UIs / metrics.

Method C++ Lua Actions sent this tick Engine::actionsSentThisTick(ctx) → int srs.engine.actionsSentThisTick() → int Per-tick action cap Engine::actionLimit(ctx) → int srs.engine.actionLimit() → int Can dispatch another? Engine::canDispatchAction(ctx) → bool srs.engine.canDispatchAction() → bool Lifetime action count Engine::totalActionsCounted(ctx) → uint64 srs.engine.totalActionsCounted() → number

canDispatchAction() is a probabilistic guard, not a guarantee — the server has the final say, and the client observes what it sent, not what the server processed. For burst-action scripts the match is much closer to engine behaviour than a blind sleep.

actionLimit() is currently the constant 8. If a future OSRS revision makes the cap per-opcode, the method signature will keep returning a single int and an opcode-aware overload will be added alongside.

script.onTick(function()
  if srs.engine.canDispatchAction() then
    srs.inventory.dropAll("Big bones")
  end
end)

docs.title: Diagnostic primitives (Lua-only)
docs.text: For RE work, one-shot probes, and scripts that need a CS2 hook the high-level API doesn't expose yet. Mirrors a subset of RuneLite's client.* surface. No C++ equivalent on srs::api::Engine — these intentionally live only in Lua so they don't accidentally become part of the production plugin contract.

docs.title: VarClient + CS2
docs.text:
Lua Description srs.engine.getVarcInt(varcId) → int or nil Read a VarClientInt. Returns nil if the id is unset. srs.engine.setVarcInt(varcId, value) → bool Write a VarClientInt. RuneLite's setVarcIntValue equivalent. srs.engine.runScript(scriptId, ...args) → bool Invoke a CS2 client script. Variadic ints only — mirrors Microbot's Client.runScript(id, args).

runScript powers things like the bank scrollbar sync (runScript(UPDATE_SCROLLBAR, ...)); use it when there's no purpose-built API for the CS2 routine you need to drive.

-- Read the current bank scroll position
local scrollY = srs.engine.getVarcInt(BANK_SCROLL_VARC)

docs.title: Input-block toggle
docs.text:
The script engine holds an input gate that prevents the user's WndProc clicks from racing the script's spoofed clicks (which would corrupt the engine's click slot mid-spoof). These two calls pop / push that gate.

Lua Description srs.engine.releaseInputBlock() Lift the gate so the user can interact with the game mid-script. srs.engine.takeInputBlock() Restore the gate.

Production scripts MUST NOT call these

Leaving user input enabled mid-spoof corrupts the engine's click slot. Use this only where you are testing something locally and want to see what value would be returned by a manual action on the client. The gate is re-taken automatically on script reload.

There is no public C++ header — plugins go through EntityQuery and ActionTarget (internal-only headers).

Name lookups are case- and whitespace-insensitive. Empty result if the cache hasn't decoded a matching NpcType yet (rare).

The global npc table (npc.all(), npc.byId(id), npc.byName(name), npc.nearest(), npc.nearestById(id), npc.nearestByName(name)) aliases the same EntityQuery backend and also returns ActionTargets. The finder surface is documented once on Npc — prefer that page for the full table.

docs.title: Radius queries
docs.text:
entity.playersWithin(x, y, radius) returns the players whose tile is within radius tiles of (x, y) measured as Chebyshev distance (max(|dx|, |dy|) — a square ring, the same metric the game uses for NPC aggression). Pass an optional 4th plane argument to restrict to a single plane; omit it for any plane. entity.npcsWithin(...) is the NPC companion — but note that visible NPC planes are currently normalized to 0, so the plane filter is effectively any-plane for NPCs (omit it).

This is the built-in form of a "count nearby players" anti-crash scan — equivalent to Microbot's playerCache.query().where(p -> p.getWorldLocation().distanceTo(t) <= r):

-- Number of OTHER players within 2 tiles of a vein
local crowd = #entity.playersWithin(vein.tileX, vein.tileY, 2)

Self-inclusion

entity.players(), entity.nearestPlayer(), and entity.playersWithin() never include the local player — the local render slot is skipped when the list is built. You do not need to hand-filter your own tile / name out of the results. If you ever need your own position, use srs.player.* (e.g. srs.player.displayName() / the player-position API), not the entity list.

docs.text:
-- Attack the nearest cow
local cow = entity.npcByName("Cow")[1]

-- Combat-style retaliation gate: is any nearby NPC fighting me?
local me = srs.player.displayName()
for _, npc in ipairs(entity.npcs()) do
    local opp = npc.interactTarget

        local players = entity.players()
        for _, p in ipairs(players) do
            if p.spawnIndex == opp and p.name == me then
                log.info("Being attacked by " .. npc.name)
                break
            end
        end
    end
end

docs.text:
srs::api::Game / srs.game

Engine-level state queries that don't belong on Player or the entity facades. Scripts use this to know whether a login screen is up, whether a logout transition is in flight, or to disambiguate login-failure modes (wrong creds vs. banned vs. not a member) by reading the live login index.

Read-only

Scripts cannot drive the login flow themselves — that's owned by Breaks / BreakManager so credentials stay sandboxed.

docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Current top-level state Game::state(ctx) → State srs.game.state() → int Human-readable label Game::stateName(s) → const char* srs.game.stateName() → string Convenience — state == LoggedIn Game::isLoggedIn(ctx) → bool srs.game.isLoggedIn() → bool Login sub-state index Game::loginIndex(ctx) → int32 srs.game.loginIndex() → int Members world? Returns -1 when the LoginIndex signature didn't resolve — in that case the BreakManager's LoginDriver falls back to widget-based detection. See the re_login_index.md memory for the value table.

docs.text:
The walk family — game.moveTo, game.walkTo, game.minimapWalkTo, game.walkFastCanvas, game.walkSmart, game.isMoving, game.hasArrived, game.cancelMove — is documented on Walk alongside the newer srs.walk facade. Two functions live only here:

Method Lua Returns Raw path query game.findPath(goalX, goalY) {found, cost, nodesExplored, path={ {x,y}, ... }} \| nil Nearest safe tile game.findSafeTile(originX, originY, dangerTiles[, radius=5[, plane=player plane]]) {x, y, plane, onCanvas, walkable} \| nil

game.findPath runs the client-side pathfinder from the player's position without moving; useful for reachability and cost checks.

game.findSafeTile searches outward in Chebyshev square rings around the origin for the nearest walkable tile not in dangerTiles (a list of {x=, y=, plane=} tables); at equal distance, a tile projectable on the canvas beats an off-canvas one. The origin itself is skipped. Three overloads: (originX, originY, dangerTiles), (…, radius), (…, radius, plane). Returns nil when no candidate within the radius qualifies.

Unified with Walk::findSafeTile

game.findSafeTile is a thin adapter over Walk::findSafeTile (Walk) — both surfaces share a single ring-search implementation, so behavior cannot drift between them. The Lua contract is unchanged: same {x, y, plane, onCanvas, walkable} table (or nil where C++ reports valid = false), and danger entries without a plane key still default to the search plane.

docs.text:
-- Dodge: step to the nearest safe tile away from two danger tiles
local me = game.playerPosition()
if me then
    local danger = {
        { x = me.x, y = me.y, plane = me.plane },
        { x = me.x + 1, y = me.y, plane = me.plane },
    }
    local safe = game.findSafeTile(me.x, me.y, danger, 4)
    if safe and safe.onCanvas then
        game.walkFastCanvas(safe.x, safe.y)
    elseif safe then
        game.moveTo(safe.x, safe.y)
    else
        log.warn("No safe tile within 4")
    end
end

docs.title: GE Prices
docs.text:
srs::api::GePrices / srs.ge

Live Grand Exchange market / guide prices, for pricing offers sensibly.

The native OSRS client has no "your price is far above the guide — are you sure?" dialog (that's a RuneLite feature), so GrandExchange::buyItem / sellItem place whatever price you pass with no safety net. These methods give scripts an independent market reference. Mirrors Microbot's Rs2GrandExchange.getRealTimePrices.

Prices are fetched client-side over HTTPS from the OSRS Wiki real-time API (with a GE-Tracker fallback) and cached per item id for 60 s. Lookups are keyed purely by item id — no ScriptContext, no login required — and are thread-safe.

Blocking — never call from draw

The first lookup for an item is a blocking HTTPS round-trip on the calling script thread (subsequent calls within the TTL hit the cache). Call from onTick / pulse / your own logic, never from the draw / onDraw callback.

Wiki API etiquette

The wiki requires a descriptive User-Agent with a contact. A default is sent; override it with setUserAgent (Lua srs.ge.setPriceUserAgent) if you distribute a script widely.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
itemId <= 0 is always invalid / 0.

Method C++ Lua Full price record GePrices::prices(itemId) → GePriceInfo srs.ge.prices(itemId) → GePriceInfo Instant-buy price (what you pay now) GePrices::buyPrice(itemId) → int32 srs.ge.buyPrice(itemId) → int Instant-sell price (what you get now) GePrices::sellPrice(itemId) → int32 srs.ge.sellPrice(itemId) → int Midpoint guide price GePrices::guidePrice(itemId) → int32 srs.ge.guidePrice(itemId) → int Adaptive buy price (widen to fill) GePrices::adaptiveBuyPrice(itemId, retry) → int32 srs.ge.adaptiveBuyPrice(itemId, retry) → int Adaptive sell price (undercut to fill) GePrices::adaptiveSellPrice(itemId, retry) → int32 srs.ge.adaptiveSellPrice(itemId, retry) → int

Scalar getters return 0 on any failure. The adaptive prices start from the instant side and widen the margin by retry (bump it each time an offer fails to fill), widening further when traded volume is thin: buy = high × (1 + margin), sell = low × (1 − margin) (floored at 1). Use them to re-list more aggressively.

docs.title: Grand Exchange
docs.text:
srs::api::GrandExchange / srs.ge

Read the player's 8 Grand Exchange offer slots and drive the GE interface. Mirrors Microbot's Rs2GrandExchange.

Offer state is read live from the engine's offer array and works whether the GE window is open or closed (the RuneLite getGrandExchangeOffers analog) — no hook, no open window required. Interaction drives the GE's CS2 interface components (offer boxes, steppers, search box) plus the keyboard subsystem for exact numeric / item-name entry.

Most interaction needs the GE open

State reads (offers, offer, hasData, the slot predicates) work anywhere. Everything that clicks — createBuyOffer, buyItem, confirm, … — needs the Grand Exchange interface open first. Open it by interacting with a GE clerk: srs.npc.interact(clerk, "Exchange") (C++ Npc::interact).

Blocking helpers

buyItem / sellItem / setQuantity / setPrice / searchItem drive a multi-step flow with internal sleeps and keyboard entry. They block the calling script thread (up to a few seconds) and mute its pulse / onTick until they return. Blocking is safe — the DoAction is marshalled to the engine thread and keystrokes post asynchronously — but never call them from draw.

These open the relevant chatbox prompt, type the value with human-paced timing, wait for the input queue to drain, and (for numbers) submit with Enter. searchItem populates the result list but does not pick a result — use buyItem for the full flow.

docs.text:
The high-level surface — find a slot, select the item, set quantity + price, confirm, all in one call. The GE offer screen must already be open.

Method C++ Lua Place a complete buy offer GrandExchange::buyItem(ctx, itemId\|name, quantity, price) → bool srs.ge.buyItem(itemId\|name, quantity, price) → bool Place a complete sell offer GrandExchange::sellItem(ctx, itemId\|name, quantity, price) → bool srs.ge.sellItem(itemId\|name, quantity, price) → bool

Both accept either an item id (number) or a display name (string) as the first argument. price is gp-per-item; pass <= 0 to leave the engine's default guide price untouched. quantity must be > 0. buyItem types the name into the search box and selects the match (the by-id form resolves the display name via the live item cache); sellItem requires the item in your backpack and picks its slot automatically. Returns true only if the flow ran through Confirm.

For sensible prices, pair these with the market-price helpers on the same srs.ge table — e.g. srs.ge.buyItem(id, qty, srs.ge.buyPrice(id)).

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Each entry (Lua: plain table; C++: GraphicsObjectEntry):

Field Type Notes id int SpotAnim cache id. animationId int The bound animation id (resolved from the spotanim's animation definition). Negative until the engine binds the animation. plane int 0..3 tileX int World tile X. tileZ int World tile Y (Z in our naming). fineX int Engine sub-tile coordinate (localTileX * 128 + 64). fineY int Engine sub-tile coordinate. height int Height value relative to the tile. startCycle int The engine cycle at which this gfx began (or will begin) rendering. The gfx is in a "pending" state until currentCycle >= startCycle, then plays for the duration baked into its animation definition. framesSinceStart int currentFrame - startCycle. Negative while pending, positive while rendering. Not a lifetime countdown — the actual end is determined by the animation's own length. finished bool true once the engine has released the bound animation (the gfx is done playing and will be pruned on the next engine tick).

docs.title: List active gfx near the player
Dodge dangerous tiles
docs.text:
A boss-mechanic dodger. Maintains a set of "lethal" spotanim ids and walks the player off any tile currently flagged as dangerous.

-- Tune for the boss you're fighting.
local DANGEROUS_IDS = { [1448]=true, [1295]=true, [1259]=true }

script.onTick(function()
    -- Build the current dangerous-tile list from live gfx.
    local danger = {}
    for _, g in ipairs(srs.graphicsObjects.all()) do
        if DANGEROUS_IDS[g.id] and not g.finished then
            danger[#danger+1] = { x=g.tileX, y=g.tileZ, plane=g.plane }
        end
    end
    if #danger == 0 then return end

    local p = srs.player.position()
    local onDanger = false
    for _, d in ipairs(danger) do
        if d.plane==p.plane and d.x==p.x and d.y==p.y then
            onDanger = true; break
        end
    end
    if not onDanger then return end

    -- Find the closest walkable safe tile and walk there.
    local safe = game.findSafeTile(p.x, p.y, danger, 5)
    if safe then
        game.walkSmart(safe.x, safe.y, safe.plane)
        log.info(string.format("Dodging to (%d, %d)", safe.x, safe.y))
    end
end)

See Walk for findSafeTile / walkSmart / walkFastCanvas documentation. Note game.findSafeTile (used above) is the Lua-side implementation on the global game table; the C++ facade counterpart is Walk::findSafeTile.

docs.title: React to a specific cast
docs.text:
Wait until a particular spotanim id appears and react once it's been rendering for a few frames.

local TARGET_ID = 1042   -- replace with the id you care about

script.onTick(function()
    for _, g in ipairs(srs.graphicsObjects.all()) do
        if g.id == TARGET_ID and g.framesSinceStart >= 0 and not g.finished then
            -- gfx is currently rendering — react now
            log.info(string.format("Target gfx active at (%d, %d)", g.tileX, g.tileZ))
            return
        end
    end
end)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• framesSinceStart is NOT a "time until removal" countdown. The engine prunes the gfx based on the animation's natural length, not from a counter on the gfx-object itself. Use finished to detect end-of-life.
  • fineX/fineY vs tileX/tileZ. Both are exposed for convenience. tileX/tileZ give world tile coordinates; fineX/fineY give the engine's sub-tile units (tile * 128 + 64). For tile-equality comparisons against Player.position(), use tileX/tileZ.
  • Pending gfx. When a spotanim has a start-delay in its packet (chained / sequenced effects), it appears in the list with framesSinceStart < 0 before it actually starts rendering. Filter on framesSinceStart >= 0 if you only care about currently-visible effects.

Input
docs.text:
srs.input (Lua only)

Low-level keyboard primitives. Used for camera-rotation calibration (measuring how long an arrow-key hold takes to rotate N yaw units) and antiban scenarios that need hand-rolled key timing rather than the all-in-one srs.camera.keyboardRotateTo* helpers.

There is no public C++ header for this surface — plugins use InputManager directly.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Lua What it does Tap a key (WndProc) srs.input.keyTap(vk, holdMs) Press now, schedule release in holdMs Tap a key (deprecated alias) srs.input.osKeyTap(vk, holdMs) Forwards to keyTap — same WndProc path Any release scheduled? srs.input.isKeyPending() → bool True if a previous tap hasn't released yet

docs.title: keyTap vs osKeyTap
docs.text:
There is now one path: all scripted input goes through WndProc (CallWindowProcW), which is per-window and so works in the background and across multiple clients. osKeyTap is a deprecated alias that forwards to keyTap — it no longer uses SendInput and has no foreground requirement. Prefer keyTap; osKeyTap is kept only so older ported scripts keep compiling.

keyTap release fires from InputManager::update() which runs every rendered frame (~16 ms granularity, driven by PathExecutor::onFrame in dllmain). holdMs < 0 is clamped to 0.

docs.text:
-- Calibrate yaw-rotation rate: hold left arrow for 1s, measure delta
local y0 = srs.camera.getYaw()
srs.input.keyTap(srs.input.VK.LEFT, 1000)
script.nextTick(function()
    local y1 = srs.camera.getYaw()
    log.info(("Δyaw over 1s = %d units"):format((y1 - y0) % 2048))
end)

Do not call dropAll again each tick to "keep dropping" — that re-queues the whole set. Fire it once, then treat the drop as finished when pendingDropCount() returns 0.

Magic

srs::api::Magic / srs.magic

Cast spells using the Spells metadata table. Widget child IDs come from RuneLite gameval/InterfaceID MagicSpellbook (group 218).

docs.text:

MenuEntry
docs.text:
srs::api::MenuEntry / srs.menuEntry

Typed fluent builder over Interact::doActionRaw. Goes through the same spoof-then-DoAction path as every other facade — fail-closed if the spoofer can't inject.

Use this when you need raw control over MenuAction params (e.g. while RE'ing a new interaction type) without bypassing the input simulation contract.

Equivalent to Microbot's NewMenuEntry, minus the option/target text fields (those route through Interact::perform's higher-level path; this builder targets the raw MenuAction dispatch path).

docs.title: NPC
docs.text:
srs::api::Npc / srs.npc

Find NPCs in the scene and act on them. The srs.npc table carries both the finders (which NPCs are nearby) and the actions (attack, talk-to, …) so scripts can stay in one table.

A target is identified by its spawn index + world coords. In C++ the finders return NpcEntry (the recommended form for new plugin code); in Lua they return the ActionTarget usertype. The action methods accept either, so srs.npc.attack(npc) / npc:attack() work on whatever a finder handed you.

All interact / attack / talkTo / bank / examine calls route through Interact, which always spoofs mouse motion + click before DoAction (no escape hatch).

The C++ side takes an NpcEntry (a legacy ActionTarget overload also exists). See Prayer for the OverheadPrayer enum values — it's a Lua global enum, not under srs.npc.

isAlive semantics

isAlive is a host-side check that the NPC's NpcInstance is still present in the world hash map. After an NPC dies it lingers a few ticks playing the death animation, then despawns — once that happens isAlive returns false. Currently does not treat HP-0-but-still-rendering as "dead"; callers that need that (loot timing, drop tracking) should poll currentHp via the NPCs panel column or entity.npcById(...).

docs.title: ActionTarget method-call shortcuts (Lua)
docs.text:
The ActionTarget usertype exposes the same set as methods:

local npc = entity.nearestNpc()
if npc and npc:isAlive() then
    npc:attack()         -- == srs.npc.attack(npc)
    npc:talkTo()
    npc:bank()
    npc:interact("Pickpocket")
    npc:overheadPrayer() -- == srs.npc.overheadPrayer(npc)
end

examine has no usertype shortcut

examine is the one action not exposed as an ActionTarget method — there is no npc:examine(). Call srs.npc.examine(npc).

docs.text:
In Lua, finders return the ActionTarget usertype. In C++, finders return NpcEntry — a plain struct with NPC-specific fields: id, spawnIndex, name, tileX, tileY, plane, animationId (−1 = idle), orientation (−1 = unknown), currentHp / maxHp (−1 = unknown), combatLevel (−1 = unknown), modelMagnitude (engine getXYZMag half-extent; 0 = unknown). The action methods accept either type.

The two fields exist on every ActionTarget, but today only the player producer fills them — NPC targets read -1 for both until the NPC-side producer is wired up. C++ NpcEntry carries the real NPC values already.

Object
docs.text:
object.* (Lua only — global table)

Live query over scene objects (trees, doors, banks, stairs, etc. — "Locs" in OSRS terminology). Distinct from entity (NPCs / players) and grounditem (lootable items on the floor).

There is no public C++ header — plugins go through ObjectQuery directly.

Global table

Lives at Lua global scope, not under srs.* — object.nearest(), not srs.object.nearest(). Kept this way for source-compat.

See also

For interaction prefer the higher-level srs.gameobject facade, which returns lighter GameObjectEntry tables and ships a built-in interact() helper.

srs::api::Player / srs.player

docs.title: Detail
docs.text:
• position — returns {0, 0, 0} when GS or the player struct isn't resolved (pre-login). Callers that care about the difference should check World::getId(ctx) >= 0 first. Inside an instance this is the raw instance-local tile.
  • templatePosition — same as position outside an instance; inside an instance it maps the raw instance-local tile back through the engine's chunk layout to the template world tile (the wiki / RuneLite / Microbot coordinate), falling back to position when the conversion can't be made. Pairs with srs.area.isInInstance() to decide raw-vs-template coordinates in instanced content.
  • displayName — empty string pre-login. Resolved via WI-map (GS+0xCA40 → WorldInstance → PlayerSubMap.find(LocalPlayerIndex)) in patch 238+.
  • animation — current animation id from the active AnimSlot. -1 = idle.
  • weight — reads VarPlayer 169.
  • runEnergy — in 0..10000 range (raw network units; divide by 100 for the displayed percentage). -1 if GS isn't resolved.
  • idleTicks — number of consecutive game ticks the player's active animation has been -1. Reset to 0 the moment any non-idle animation plays. Maintained by GameData::onTick.
  • skillLevel / skillBase / skillXp — read the boosted level, base level, or total XP for any skill. Returns 0 when GS isn't resolved.
  • hitpoints / maxHitpoints — shorthand for skillLevel(Skill::Hitpoints) / skillBase(Skill::Hitpoints).
  • prayer / maxPrayer — current prayer points (live, drains with use) + base prayer level. Mirrors srs::api::Prayer::points / Prayer::level.
  • overheadPrayer — the local player's active Protect-from headicon. OverheadPrayer.None when no overhead prayer is active or pre-login. See Prayer for the OverheadPrayer enum (a Lua global enum — same values for players and NPCs; NPCs read it via Npc::overheadPrayer).
  • questState — completion bucket for a quest (NotStarted / InProgress / Finished). Backed by the engine's QUEST_STATUS_GET clientscript (CS2 4029) — the same source RuneLite/Microbot use — so it is correct for every quest with no hand-maintained thresholds. The script must run on the engine thread while scripts run on the render thread, so the value is cached and refreshed asynchronously on the engine thread (EngineDispatch's non-click work lane, drained on every outbound packet): the first lookup of a given quest returns QuestState::Unknown and kicks off a refresh that lands within a tick or two on its own — no click needed, then stays live. Poll until != Unknown, or just read it each tick. Subsequent reads are instant.
  • questProgress — the raw varbit/varp that increments as a quest advances (RuneLite QuestVarbits / QuestVarPlayer) — i.e. the step number a questing script wants. Thread-safe and instant (a plain var read, no clientscript). 0 before the quest is started; quest-specific value as it advances; -1 for the handful of quests with no single tracked progress var, or when VarpSystem isn't ready. Use questState for completion; use this for "which step am I on".

docs.title: Example
PluginSettings
docs.text:
srs::api::PluginSettings

Write back to your plugin (or Lua script's) own schema-driven settings — the flat "<groupId>.<rowId>" values that back the schema returned by IScript::schema() / declared by script.declareSettings.

Different from srs::api::Settings, which reads GAME settings (varbits / varps). This module is about the plugin/script's own UI values.

Ctx-less by design — mirrors Lua's script.setSetting, which also takes no ctx. The write is attributed to the currently firing plugin (the one whose method is running on the calling thread). Meaningful during onSettingsButton / onSettingsChanged / pulse / onTick / onDraw; a call from outside a callback context is silently dropped.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Register a button handler PluginSettings::onButton(action, fn) → void script.onSettingsButton(name, fn) Write one flat setting PluginSettings::setValue(key, value) → void script.setSetting(key, value)

The Lua bindings live in the script.* namespace since scripts already have a script global; C++ plugins reach the same behavior via the free functions above.

Register from onLoad. onButton uses the same thread_local attribution as setValue, and onLoad runs with the plugin attributed. Registering elsewhere works too (any callback), but onLoad is the natural one-time home. fn is std::function<void(const std::string& action, const ScriptContext& ctx)>.

ABI note. This is a registered-callback API (not an IScript virtual) specifically so adding it never shifted the IScript vtable. Plugins built against an older SDK header keep loading — they simply don't register any buttons. Extend IScript itself only by appending at the end.

key is "<groupId>.<rowId>" — the same flat encoding onSettingsChanged receives. value may be any JSON-representable value that matches the row's kind: bool for check, number for number / slider, string for text / select. Written values persist per in-game character.

docs.title: Example — gear-setup capture button
docs.text:
A button row + a text row let a plugin snapshot the currently worn gear into a textbox:

C++Lua 
#include "PluginAPI/API/PluginSettings.h"
#include "PluginAPI/API/Equipment.h"

class GearCapture : public IScript {
public:
    const char* name() const override { return "Gear Capture"; }
    void onUnload() override {}

    bool onLoad(const ScriptContext&) override {
        // Register the button handler once. Attribution is automatic —
        // onLoad runs with this plugin as the currently-firing one.
        srs::api::PluginSettings::onButton("pull_gear",
            [](const std::string& /*action*/, const ScriptContext& ctx) {
                std::string ids;
                for (auto& e : srs::api::Equipment::all(ctx)) {
                    if (!ids.empty()) ids += ',';
                    ids += std::to_string(e.id);
                }
                srs::api::PluginSettings::setValue("gear.ids", ids);
            });
        return true;
    }

    nlohmann::json schema() const override {
        return {{"groups", {{
            {"id", "gear"}, {"title", "gear setup"}, {"open", true},
            {"rows", {
                {{"id","ids"},  {"label","Equipped item ids"}, {"kind","text"},
                 {"value",""},  {"placeholder","click Pull to fill"}, {"mono", true}},
                {{"id","pull"}, {"label","Fill from worn gear"}, {"kind","button"},
                 {"value","Pull equipped"}, {"action","pull_gear"}},
            }}
        }}}};
    }
};

script.declareSettings {
  groups = {
    { id = "gear", title = "gear setup", open = true, rows = {
      { id = "ids",  label = "Equipped item ids", kind = "text",
        value = "", placeholder = "click Pull to fill", mono = true },
      { id = "pull", label = "Fill from worn gear", kind = "button",
        value = "Pull equipped", action = "pull_gear" },
    }},
  },
}

script.onSettingsButton("pull_gear", function()
  local ids = {}
  for _, e in ipairs(srs.equipment.all()) do ids[#ids + 1] = e.id end
  script.setSetting("gear.ids", table.concat(ids, ","))
end)

docs.title: Threading
docs.text: Button clicks (and therefore PluginSettings::setValue calls made from inside onSettingsButton) run on the ScriptScheduler worker, never the render thread. A slow handler (item-name load, GE / bank calls) cannot freeze the game. Blocking primitives inside the handler release the GIL via the usual helpers so the render thread's onDraw / Lua script.draw keeps running smoothly.

docs.text:
srs::api::OverheadPrayer / Lua global OverheadPrayer

The overhead protection-prayer headicon shown above an actor. In C++ this is a pure enum header (OverheadPrayer.h — no class, no export):

    None = -1, Melee = 0, Missiles = 1, Magic = 2,

In Lua the enum is registered at global scope — write OverheadPrayer.Missiles, not srs.prayer.OverheadPrayer (no such path exists).

Projectiles
docs.text:
srs::api::Projectiles / srs.projectiles

Read-only enumeration of in-flight projectiles. The common case is "what's about to hit me and when" — use incoming() for that.

Cache ids

id is this client's spotanim/graphic cache id (cache group 0xD in the OSRS-OS3303-BWXF build). It does not directly equal RuneLite's ProjectileID enum — different cache revisions diverge by varying amounts. If you need RuneLite-style labels, build a per-build mapping table.

Time units

ticksUntilLanding is in game ticks (600 ms each, rounded up from the underlying ~30-frame-per-tick counter at GS+0x2154).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Any incoming projectile (cheap) Projectiles::isUnderFire(ctx) → bool srs.projectiles.isUnderFire() → bool Incoming list Projectiles::incoming(ctx) → vector<ProjectileEntry> srs.projectiles.incoming() → table Next-to-land Projectiles::next(ctx) → optional<ProjectileEntry> srs.projectiles.next() → table \| nil Ticks until next Projectiles::ticksUntilNext(ctx) → int32 srs.projectiles.ticksUntilNext() → int All projectiles scene-wide (heavier) Projectiles::all(ctx) → vector<ProjectileEntry> srs.projectiles.all() → table
  • isUnderFire is allocation-free — preferred for tight check-loops.
  • next is the lowest absoluteEndCycle.
  • ticksUntilNext returns -1 when nothing is in flight (single int compare instead of optional unwrap, for ranged-prayer flick logic).
  • all is heavier than incoming — walks the WI hashmap.

docs.title: Spawn events
docs.text:
Method C++ Lua Subscribe to projectile spawns Projectiles::onSpawned(cb) → uint64 srs.projectiles.onSpawned(fn) → token Unsubscribe Projectiles::offSpawned(token) srs.projectiles.offSpawned(token) → bool

onSpawned fires the instant the engine constructs a projectile — for every projectile in the scene, not just ones aimed at you.

C++: process-wide, takes no ScriptContext; returns a token (0 if the hook isn't installed) to pass to offSpawned. The callback (ProjectileSpawnedCallback = std::function<void(const ProjectileSpawnedEvent&)>) runs on the game thread, synchronously — keep it cheap and thread-safe.

Lua: fn receives a table {id, cycle, pos0, pos1, pos2, wallClock}. onSpawned returns a numeric token; pass it to offSpawned to unsubscribe.

Unsubscribing

srs.projectiles.offSpawned(token) removes the callback registered under that token. It is safe to call from inside the callback itself (one-shot listeners). Returns false for an unknown or already-removed token. A full script reload still clears all subscriptions automatically, so a register-once-at-load callback needs no explicit cleanup.

Script lifecycle
docs.text:
script.* / log.* / srs.wait (Lua — global tables)

Everything a Lua script uses to hook into the engine: lifecycle callbacks, script metadata + settings, logging, tick suspension, and the sandboxed module loader. There is no srs::api facade for this surface — C++ plugins implement the IScript virtuals (onLoad / onTick / pulse / onDraw) directly instead.

docs.title: Lifecycle callbacks
docs.text:
Method Lua Notes Per-frame callback (~60 Hz) script.pulse(fn) Runs every render frame Per-game-tick callback (~600 ms) script.onTick(fn) Runs once per server tick One-shot next-tick callback script.nextTick(fn) Fires once on the next tick rollover Overlay draw callback script.draw(fn) Per-frame, inside a live ImGui frame — srs.draw / srs.overlay are only valid here

pulse and onTick are both optional — register whichever cadence fits. Use onTick for game logic (actions, state machines) and pulse only when you genuinely need frame-rate polling.

docs.title: Metadata and settings
docs.text: Method Lua Notes Declare settings schema script.declareSettings(schemaTable) Top-level only — silently no-ops outside script load Declare script info script.declareInfo({name=, author=, version=, description=}) Top-level only Read current settings script.settings() → table Empty table if the calling script can't be attributed Settings-changed callback script.onSettingsChanged(fn(settingsTable)) Fires when the user edits settings in the client UI Settings button handler script.onSettingsButton(name, fn) Top-level only — runs fn when the user clicks a button row whose action equals name Set one setting value script.setSetting("group.row", value) Writes a flat value back to the UI + saved config; use inside a button handler

docs.title: Settings schema shape
docs.text:
declareSettings takes { groups = { … } }; each group is { id, title, open, rows = { … } } and each row is { id, label, kind, … }. Settings are stored flat as "<groupId>.<rowId>" and saved per in-game character — different characters keep independent configs.

Supported row kinds:

kind Extra fields Renders as check — Toggle select options (strings or {id,label}) Dropdown number min, max, step, suffix Numeric field (with unit suffix) slider min, max, step, suffix Slider with its value shown next to the track text placeholder, maxLength, mono Text field (own line; mono = monospace, for id lists) button action, value (button caption) Button — holds no value; clicking fires onSettingsButton(action)

C++ plugins have the same surface

The Lua script.onSettingsButton / script.setSetting map to the IScript::onSettingsButton(action, ctx) virtual and the srs::api::PluginSettings::setValue(key, value) free function. The schema shape (row kinds, per-character storage, worker-thread dispatch) is identical.

docs.title: Gear-setup example
docs.text:
A button row + a text row let a script pull the currently worn gear into a textbox:

script.declareSettings({
  groups = {
    { id = "gear", title = "gear setup", open = true, rows = {
      { id = "ids",  label = "Equipped item ids", kind = "text",
        placeholder = "click Pull to fill", mono = true },
      { id = "pull", label = "Fill from worn gear", kind = "button",
        value = "Pull equipped", action = "pull_gear" },
    }},
  },
})

script.onSettingsButton("pull_gear", function()
  local ids = {}
  for _, e in ipairs(srs.equipment.all()) do ids[#ids + 1] = e.id end
  script.setSetting("gear.ids", table.concat(ids, ","))
end)

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Method Lua Notes Info line log.info(msg) Appends [INFO] msg to the engine output buffer Warning line log.warn(msg) [WARN] prefix Error line log.error(msg) [ERROR] prefix Print print(...) Overridden: tab-concatenated tostring() of each arg, to the engine output buffer — not stdout

The only logging APIs

log.info/warn/error and the overridden print are the whole surface. There is no srs.log.* and no osrs.print — code using those names errors at call time.

docs.title: Waits (tick suspension)
docs.text:
Method Lua Notes Wait N ticks srs.wait([ticks=1]) Mutes this script for N ticks Wait for condition srs.waitUntil(predicateFn[, timeoutTicks=0]) timeoutTicks=0 = no timeout

wait is a suspension gate, not a coroutine sleep

srs.wait(n) mutes this script's pulse / onTick / nextTick callbacks for n ticks — draw keeps firing. It does not interrupt the currently running callback: code after the call still executes. The idiom is srs.wait(n); return. Both wait and waitUntil are silent no-ops outside a firing callback.

  • srs.waitUntil(fn) releases when the predicate returns truthy; if the predicate throws, the wait releases (fail-open) rather than hanging the script.
  • There is no global sleep or scriptSleep.

docs.title: Module loading (require)
docs.text:
require(mod) is replaced with a sandboxed bundle loader:

  • require("a.b") resolves a/b.lua, then a/b/init.lua, from the current bundle's in-memory files only — no filesystem access, no loadlib.
  • Results are cached per bundle; requiring the same module twice returns the cached value.
  • Calling require outside a bundle context (e.g. from a single-file script) or for a missing module throws an error.

docs.title: Available Lua stdlib
docs.text: Open libraries: base, string, math, table, os. Not available: io, package (require is replaced — see above).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
script.declareInfo{ name = "Miner", author = "me", version = "1.0",
                    description = "Powermines iron" }

script.onTick(function()
    if srs.inventory.isFull() then
        srs.inventory.dropAll("Iron ore")
        srs.wait(2)  -- mute onTick for 2 ticks; code below still runs
        return
    end
    log.info("Ticking, slots free: " .. srs.inventory.emptySlots())
end)

script.draw(function()
    -- srs.draw / srs.overlay calls are valid only here
end)
